In [[mathematics]], a '''branched surface''' is a generalization of both [[surface (topology)|surface]]s and [[train track (mathematics)|train track]]s.

==Definition==
A [[Surface (topology)|surface]] is a space that locally looks like <math>\mathbb{R}^2</math> ([[homeomorphic]] to the [[Euclidean plane]]). 

Consider, however, the space obtained by taking the  [[Quotient space (topology)|quotient]] of two copies A,B of <math>\mathbb{R}^2</math> under the identification of a closed [[Half-space (geometry)|half-space]] of each with a closed half-space of the other. This will be a surface except along a single line. Now, pick another copy C of <math>\mathbb{R}</math> and glue it and A together along halfspaces so that the singular line of this gluing is transverse in A to the previous singular line.

Call this complicated space K. A '''branched surface''' is a space that is locally modeled on K.<ref>Li, Tao. "Laminar Branched Surfaces in 3-manifolds." Geometry and Topology 6.153 (2002): 194.</ref>

==Weight==
A branched manifold can have a '''weight''' assigned to various of its [[Topological subspace#Constructing_new_topological_spaces_from_given_ones|subspaces]]; if this is done, the space is often called a '''weighted branched manifold'''.<ref>Shields, Sandra. "The stability of foliations of orientable 3-manifolds covered by a product." Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 348.11 (1996): 4653-4671.</ref> Weights are non-negative [[real number]]s and are assigned to subspaces ''N'' that satisfy the following:
*''N'' is open.
*''N'' does not include any points whose only neighborhoods are the quotient space described above.
*''N'' is maximal with respect to the above two conditions.

That is, ''N'' is a component of the branched surface minus its branching set. Weights are assigned so that if a component branches into two other components, then the sum of the weights of the two unidentified halfplanes of that neighborhood is the weight of the identified halfplane.
